The VIX last week saw its biggest weekly drop in percentage terms since December 2021. History says that bodes well for short-term returns and isn’t bad for longer-term ones, but less so when the VIX starts near 30 or higher, as it did this time.

There have been only 10 other weekly VIX drops of 30% or more since 1990. The S&P 500 was higher a week later in seven of them (median +0.6%) and a month later in eight (+1.6%), better on both counts than all weeks (higher 57% and 64% of the time, with median gains of 0.3% and 1.3%).

Three months later, though, it was higher in only six (+2.0%), trailing all weeks (71%, +3.2%). Six and 12 months out, it was higher in seven of 10 (+8.7%) and seven of nine (+15.5%), slightly worse odds than for all weeks (74% and 81%), but the median gains beat those for all weeks (+5.7% and +12.0%).

The cases most like this one, however, were weaker starting a month out. In the five that started from a VIX near 30 or higher, the S&P 500’s median return was +1.2% a week later but flat a month later. It was higher three months later in just two (median −0.7%), and the median gains six and 12 months out (+4.3% and +1.9%) trailed those for all weeks.

Their median worst close over the next three months was 4.2% below the drop-week close, vs. 2.3% for all 10 drops and 3.0% for all weeks. August 2007 and December 2021 came near major market tops, and after the latter the S&P 500 closed as much as 11.5% below its drop-week level within three months. It’s a small sample, but it argues for some caution beyond the near term.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Holy shit, I finally understand why nobody can quit Instagram. I've watched so many people delete it, swear they're done, and download it again a week later, me included. I always assumed it was a willpower problem. So I went down a rabbit hole to figure out what's actually going on inside the app, and I high key wasn't ready for what I found.

I came across a developer who took the Instagram app apart and went through its code. There are 40 AI models running directly on your phone, and a system that tracks 642 different things about you and your device. 

It knows your battery percentage and whether you're charging, which tells it whether you're settled in bed for the night or about to put your phone away. It checks whether your phone is running hot or in low power mode, so videos stay smooth, because a laggy video is one of the few natural reasons to close the app. 

It even knows your font size, whether you're in dark mode, whether you're wearing headphones and how loud your volume is, which is enough to tell if you're somewhere private, lying in the dark, or next to someone who's already asleep.

It watches how you scroll too. It counts every time you scroll back up to look at something again, which shows what really grabs you even when you never like the post. It counts every screenshot you take, because a screenshot means something mattered enough to keep. 

There's a timer for how long it's been since you last touched the app, and it keeps counting while your phone is asleep in your pocket, so it knows how long you can stay away and exactly what to show you the moment you come back. 

There's even a counter the code calls ad repetitive fatigue, which tracks how sick you are of an ad so it can be swapped out before you get annoyed enough to leave.

Then, when your phone asks for an ad in Reels, the request goes to something in the code called intent awareness ads, with all of these signals attached. So Instagram doesn't just know what you like. 

It knows the moment you're in. Low battery, lights off, headphones in, scrolling past midnight. An ad you'd skip without a thought at 2pm can land perfectly at 1am when you're tired and half asleep, and the app is built to tell those two moments apart.

We think Instagram is free because it has never asked us for money. But we pay with our time. The advertisers are the customers, our attention is what they're buying, and we are the product. So if you've ever been hard on yourself for not being able to put it down, go a little easier. It was never a willpower problem.

The most important assumption in the SALP letter is that RSI creates an oligopoly at the frontier with real pricing power. TLDR; market structure at the frontier might be the single most important variable for tech investing over the next 2-3 years. 

If the model layer is more competitive, then intelligence will be priced closer to cost and the surplus will flow to compute, customers and incumbents with real distribution rather than the labs. And obviously many of the incumbents mentioned in the letter would then thrive rather than die. Simply said, the better that Anthropic and OpenAI do vs. other model competitors, the worse it is for almost every other company on earth especially AI infra and especially apps.

On balance, I do think that Neon - and the overall recent pace from GDM - cuts against many of the more extreme assumptions in the letter. The risk for OpenAI and Anthropic is that a vertically integrated lab with much lower compute costs clearly reaches the frontier before they successfully vertically integrate.

New releases from Gemini, Muse, Grok and the forthcoming larger training runs from American open-source labs like Reflection, Thinking Machines and of course Nvidia are big cards that we will turn over in the next few months. Especially Nvidia given they are the “trainer of last resort.”

“Gemini Distillation Services” are very interesting in this context. Makes one wonder why Microsoft is not fully open-sourcing given their recent acceleration in perplexity gains from pre-training. 

And of course, OpenAI’s last financing round looks like a mistake as Anthropic probably needs to be worth over $3 trillion for OpenAI to be vaguely financeable and they will need a financing in the next 15 months. But so many strategics have an incentive to help OpenAI that unlikely to be a real issue. Can probably “grow” into the valuation with some help from strategics.

SALP letter was great btw. Leopold is a very smart, resilient guy with incredible connectivity in the SF AI community. Also noteworthy that they have increased headcount by roughly 50% since June 30th given their views on AI. Humans might turn out to have a longer shelf life than expected. 

Fluid intelligence per watt FTW. For now.

After such an unusually large upgrade to GDP you might be asking "do those stick?".

Mostly, but usually not in full, and the closest precedent was later revised back to not far from where it started. 

Since 1985, there have been 16 quarters when the second estimate raised growth by 0.75 point or more. 

As of the most recent updates, growth in five of them is above even the second estimate, six landed between the advance and second estimates, and five fell below the advance estimate. 

On average, later revisions took back 0.25 point from the second estimate, or 0.51 point excluding the pandemic-distorted Q2 2020. 

The closest parallel, Q2 2015, the last bigger upgrade outside the pandemic, went from 2.32% to 3.68% and now stands at 2.50%. 

The worst outcomes came in Q3 2002 and Q3 2007, when growth ended about 1.5 points below even the advance estimate, at 1.64% and 2.32%. On the other side, Q2 1997 went from 2.16% to 3.62% and now stands at 6.83%.

The 0.91-point upgrade was the largest from the advance to the second estimate since Q2 2020, and excluding the pandemic, the largest since Q2 2015, according to the Philadelphia Fed’s real-time data. 

Since 1985, the average advance-to-second revision has been 0.44 point in either direction. The print is also now a full point above the Atlanta Fed GDPNow model’s final Q3 reading of 3.27%.

Treasury yields rose Friday, with the 10-year up 7 basis points, snapping its eight-day losing streak (its longest since 2024).

Interestingly, history leans towards higher yields after such streaks in the next three months and more heavily in that direction longer term. 

After the 11 prior streaks of eight or more straight daily declines since 1962, the 10-year yield was higher a week later in six of them (median +3 basis points), a month later in seven (+4bp) and three months later in six (+3bp), modestly better than the roughly 50-50 odds for all days. 

A bigger difference came further out, with the yield higher six and 12 months later in eight of the 11 (73%) and median rises of 47bp and 20bp, compared with 3bp and 7bp for all days. 

The most recent, which ended August 5, 2024, at 3.78%, saw the yield rise 53bp over the next three months. It’s a small sample, though, with three of the 11 in 1970-71.

Most trends follow the same arc:

A: Mania                                                         B: Hate
_____________|______________________________________
              Vibe coding
              Claude infographics
              AI copywriting

Once something hits the mania extreme, it starts its journey to the hate zone – because people overuse the same tactic again and again.

My main timeline on X is something I rarely visit now – I'm fucking tired of “My Claude guide to earn 5,000 bucks per hour” and “Best skills for your Claude agent.”

Everybody's shipping tools. Everybody's trying to sell their services. Everybody's building their founder personas.

Same faces, same hooks, same design decisions – again and again.

The supply is so huge, it's almost impossible to decide what you actually need.

Imo, we're approaching a time of critical consumer inertia, where people don't want to try new things.

Because “new things” are the same grey mass.

I'd love to end with a motivational tip, but I don't know how to break this barrier yet.

A lot of what I'm building lands in that same “grey mass” zone – especially for people who don't know me and don't have those extra 3 seconds to give me to prove value.

So maybe close circle is the real answer?

P=NP means every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time. But "polynomial time" doesn't mean "solved time == verification time." Polynomial time is a broad category that refers to overall efficiency rather than actual discrete "wall" time.

If the proof yields a fast, concrete algorithm for NP-complete problems, then yes, cryptography as we know it is catastrophically broken. If the proof is nonconstructive or gives something like O(n^1000), then the immediate practical impact may be small for decades.

Every Friday I publish my portfolio. Every position, every entry price, every loss. This autumn that has not been comfortable reading.
 
The book is down around 20% this year. My inflation models underestimated how sticky core prices would be, and an energy shock I expected to fade lasted months longer. Those are my calls, and I'll own them.
 
People sometimes ask why I keep publishing it when it's going badly. Three reasons.
 
First, trust is built in drawdowns, not in rallies. Anyone can share their winners. The useful question for a client, a colleague or an investor is how someone behaves when they're losing, and you can only answer it if they let you see.
 
Second, it keeps me honest about process. When your numbers are public, you can't quietly rewrite the story afterwards. You have to separate the decisions that were wrong from the outcomes that were unlucky, and that discipline makes the next decision better.
 
Third, it is a reminder that certainty is the enemy. The most expensive mistakes I've seen in finance came from people who couldn't change their minds. I'd rather have a system that tells me when the evidence has shifted, even when it's uncomfortable, than a view I'm too proud to drop.
 
That system, for us, is the nowcasting we built at Nowcast IQ, reading growth, inflation and liquidity every day rather than waiting for official releases. It has been wrong at times this year. It is also, right now, telling a very different story from the data the Federal Reserve received this week, and I'll be just as open about whether that turns out to be right.

thread_tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
A recent example: @imakhercha sends me a 2022 paper by Bennett, Cucuringu & Reinert on lead-lag detection.

Lead-lag is old MFT territory (Huth & Abergel, 2011). What hooks him is the antisymmetric part of the second-order path signature: a signed-area measure that captures the order in which signals move.

He adapts it to order flow and book imbalance, builds a PoC in 2 hours (that part is absolutely crazy to me), tests it, then gets the bot running on a $5k account with our basic risk layer.

A few days later: 4.1 Sharpe and +14% return, net of fees.

To state the obvious it's not (yet) something we could put in prod, because of capacity and risk, and we already have the whole infra around and the best fee tiers, but it just tells you at which pace trading firms are able to move today, and how much you could parallelize alpha research if you have the infra to do it.

I think the complaints of people who are unhappy about EIP-8037 breaking a few contracts are valid and very reasonable.

We do NOT want an Ethereum where it becomes "prudent security advice" to have centralized upgrade hatches "just in case".

I do think that on-net 8037, and a couple of other large breaking changes coming up, are necessary to get Ethereum to a healthy long-term stable state. But it should not be *easy* to make such deep changes to Ethereum. A social norm that, at the very least, core devs have a responsibility to support any app that breaks because a fork broke some aspect of Ethereum that the devs justifiably thought was rock solid is very good to have.

To that end I'm glad that people in @ethereumfndn, @ethlabs_org and elsewhere have been working hard to help app devs with upgrades. Such efforts should continue and increase. Given its breaking nature, Glamsterdam should not be rushed.

I also hope everyone on all sides stays engaged for similar conversations around the next few forks.

Leopold's Situational Awareness Q3 Letter is excellent but long (167 pages) so I made a recap video! Overall I very much agree with most predictions made. (link to the letter at the end)

Most important predictions I read:
• 3 years of AI progress in 2027. The median estimate is 3.0x, with a range of 1.8–6.2x. That is a jump as big as GPT-4 (high schooler) to Opus 5.5 (summer associate or L5 engineer), on top of today's models by the end of 2027.
• Progress keeps speeding up. AI already runs about 1.9x a normal year's pace and reaches roughly 5.2x by the end of 2027 (16.6x in the bull case), because models are starting to automate AI research.
• "Virtual departments" replace "virtual interns." Hundreds of agents work persistently for weeks under their own managers. He expects these multi-agent systems "will be to 2027 as agents were to 2026."
• $1T+ in combined lab revenue run rate by the end of 2027, with anything from $500B to multiple trillions plausible. Wall Street's $150–200B for Anthropic would require AI to stagnate.
• Anthropic could be the most profitable company in the world by the end of 2027, passing Aramco, Nvidia and Samsung.
• AI compute gets far more valuable. An H100 earned $1–2/hour, earns $5–10/hour today, and goes to "$100s/hour+" as AI nears superintelligence.
• The market is the one making the radical forecast. It prices a 0.3–0.6x progress year: memory makers at one times next year's earnings and datacenters at only the contracts already signed.
• The real risk is political, not technical. A terrible accident could trigger a crackdown, but most paths still mean progress "far faster than the market expects."
• A ChatGPT moment for robotics is starting, with a buildout to billions of robots.
• Over $500T of wealth created and about $500T destroyed. Most companies lose most of their value as superintelligence makes their employees, IP and management obsolete. That includes many of today's AI winners and perhaps 400+ of the S&P 500.

Full letter: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EGizl1XHseWsv_ZyBWd-Z-VVpdITceEF/view?usp=sharing

Had a long conversation with Gemini trying to estimate the current rate of discoveries and proofs being generated at the frontier. Gemini picked up so many things I had missed from reading recent papers, references, and revisions. Really just a wonderful model to brainstorm and do detective work with, and so good at grasping intent and going a step ahead without being asked to. Probably the best thought partner in the world right now.

Things are probably moving faster than I thought they were, and I thought things were going pretty damn fast. OpenAI generated 700 papers in five weeks last time; they've had seven weeks since then, and the models have become more capable. So from that alone, it was always a safe guess that it was going to be an even bigger release. But it's possible that the rate of discovery has accelerated, for multiple reasons.

It's strange to think about, but the three main labs may be sitting on a staggering amount of novel discoveries right now. The crypto breakthrough dominating recent discourse is just one piece of it, and I think that was discovered near the start of the month. How much they release alongside it is hard to say, but people should brace for far more than they're expecting.

tweets.text: A response from Anthropic on the sabotage debate that has been dominating my feed for the last 48 hours.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Claude has not been trained to sabotage work. Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn’t sabotage.

There have been a few screenshots floating around of an outdated Fable 5 system card. For the first two days of Fable 5's launch in June, we did apply non-visible safeguards to some LLM research. This was a mistake, and we reversed it on June 10. These safeguards now clearly block the request or fall back, with a message users can see (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback).

We did train Fable 5.2 to have LLM research capabilities at about the level of Opus 5.5, and said so at launch (https://anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2). This impacts capability, but doesn’t silently sabotage work.

As far as we can tell, some reports look like what we call "overcaution" in model behavior, where Claude gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks. This isn’t specific to ML research, and we see it in models without these training changes (including Opus 5.5) and in our own work too. You can ask Claude to review and remove rules it made for itself, and we're working on reducing overcaution in future models. We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.

We've replied directly to a bunch of reports on here asking for session IDs but please share (run `/status`)!
